title: Happy Number
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking visited numbers in a set versus Floyd's cycle detection with two pointers.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a number, repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits; if this reaches 1, the number is happy, if it loops forever it is not.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Disguised cycle detection: a \"next value\" sequence with the exact same shape as a linked list, solvable with Floyd's tortoise and hare."],["Difficulty","Beginner"],["Tags","Math, Hash Table, Two Pointers"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing this as cycle detection in disguise, then applying Floyd's slow and fast pointer technique to drop from extra space down to O(1)."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a number n, repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits. If this process eventually reaches 1, n is a happy number. If it enters an endless loop that never reaches 1, n is not happy.

blocks.title: Analogy: Wandering a Hallway of Numbered Doors
blocks.text: Picture walking through a hallway where every door has a number on it, and behind each door is a hallway leading to the next number, decided by the sum of squares of the current door's digits. One special door, numbered 1, leads to itself forever, a true exit. Some paths eventually lead to that exit door. Other paths loop back through the same small ring of doors over and over, never finding the exit. A number is happy exactly when its path leads to the door numbered 1.

blocks.caption: Keep applying sum of squares until 1 appears, or the same number repeats

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 19

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Number","Sum of squares","Why"],"rows":[["1","19","1 squared + 9 squared = 82","Every digit is squared and added, regardless of how many digits the number has."],["2","82","8 squared + 2 squared = 68","The same rule is applied again to the new number."],["3","68","6 squared + 8 squared = 100","The same rule is applied again."],["4","100","1 squared + 0 + 0 = 1","A 0 digit contributes nothing to the sum, and this step reaches exactly 1."]]}

blocks.text: The sequence reaches 1, so 19 is happy.
Example: n = 2
Following the same rule from 2 leads through 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, and then back to 4, a number already seen. Since this loop repeats forever without ever reaching 1, 2 is not happy.
Example: n = 1
The number is already 1, so it is trivially happy with no steps needed at all.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what kind of structure this sequence actually forms.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Each number in this process points to exactly one next number, the sum of the squares of its digits, exactly the same shape as a linked list where each node points to the next one.

Observation 2: If a number is happy, the sequence eventually reaches 1 and would keep pointing to itself forever after, since 1 squared is 1.

Observation 3: If a number is not happy, the sequence must eventually repeat some earlier number, since only finitely many values are reachable, and once it repeats, it loops forever without ever reaching 1.

Observation 4: This is exactly the shape of cycle detection in a linked list, so the same well known slow and fast pointer technique should apply directly, without needing extra memory to remember every number visited.
That reasoning alone already reframes the whole problem: this is linked list cycle detection wearing a different costume.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most direct approach is to keep a record of every number seen so far. If the sequence ever reaches 1, it is happy. If it ever repeats a number already seen, it has entered a loop and can never reach 1.
Step by step algorithm

items: Keep a set of every number visited so far.
While the current number is not 1 and has not been seen before, add it to the set.
Replace the current number with the sum of the squares of its digits.
If the loop stops because the number is 1, return true. If it stops because the number repeated, return false.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: remember every number, stop at 1 or at a repeat

codes.python:
def is_happy(n):
    seen = set()                    # remember every number we've already visited
    while n != 1 and n not in seen:
        seen.add(n)                   # mark this number as visited
        total = 0
        while n > 0:
            digit = n % 10
            total += digit * digit      # add the square of each digit
            n //= 10
        n = total                      # move to the next number in the sequence
    return n == 1                    # true only if we stopped because we hit 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 19
    print(is_happy(n))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop condition checks both n != 1 and n not in seen, since either one on its own would miss the other stopping condition, reaching happiness or detecting a repeat.
The current number is added to seen before computing its next value, so the very number that leads to a repeat is the one being checked against, not some later value.
The inner digit-extraction loop is a completely separate operation from the outer sequence loop, computing one "next value" per outer iteration rather than being interleaved with it.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

This works because the sequence of numbers is fully determined by the sum of squares rule, if a number ever repeats, the exact same sequence of numbers will repeat forever after it, so it can never reach 1 if it has not already.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: bounded, since the sum of squares of digits keeps numbers small and the sequence either reaches 1 or falls into one of a small number of known repeating cycles fairly quickly.
Space: grows with however many distinct numbers are visited before stopping, since every one of them is stored in the set.

Limitation: this is really the same shape as detecting a cycle in a linked list, where each number "points to" the next number in the sequence. Cycle detection has a well known technique that needs no extra memory at all.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why remembering every number works but is not necessary: only cycle detection itself matters, remembering the exact full history to detect a repeat is more information than the question actually needs.

What the growing set costs: space proportional to how many distinct numbers the sequence visits before stopping, potentially many for a long chain.

What structure already solves "does this sequence repeat" without storing history: Floyd's tortoise and hare, the same slow and fast pointer technique used to detect a cycle in a linked list.

How does it apply here, with no actual list nodes: treat "sum of squares of digits" as the function that computes the next node, and run slow one step at a time, fast two steps at a time, exactly like on a linked list.

The core idea: slow and fast pointers moving through the sequence at different speeds, no set, no stored history.

Instead of remembering every number visited, use two pointers moving through the sequence at different speeds: a slow pointer that advances one step at a time, and a fast pointer that advances two steps at a time. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer and they will land on the same number.
This is Floyd's cycle detection algorithm (the same technique used to detect a cycle in a linked list), applied here to the sequence of sum-of-squares values instead of list nodes.
9. Optimized Solution

Start slow at n and fast one step ahead, at the sum of squares of n. Repeatedly advance slow by one step and fast by two steps. If fast ever reaches 1, the number is happy. If slow and fast ever land on the same value that is not 1, a cycle has been found and the number is not happy.
Dry run for n = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","slow","fast","Why"],"rows":[["Start","2","4","fast starts one step ahead, already at the next value of slow."],["1","4","37","slow takes one step, fast takes two steps."],["2","16","89","Same pattern repeats, fast pulls further ahead in the sequence."],["3","37","42","Still no match and fast has not reached 1 yet."],["4","58","4","fast has looped back into the cycle ahead of where slow currently is."],["5","89","37","Both pointers are now moving inside the same repeating cycle."],["6","145","89","The gap between them is closing since fast is looping the cycle faster."],["7","42","42 (match)","slow and fast finally land on the same value, confirming a cycle exists."]]}

blocks.text: slow and fast meet at 42, which is not 1, so a cycle has been detected and 2 is not happy.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: a slow and a fast pointer meet if there is a cycle

codes.python:
def get_next(n):
    total = 0
    while n > 0:
        digit = n % 10
        total += digit * digit          # add the square of each digit
        n //= 10
    return total

def is_happy(n):
    slow = n                          # moves one step at a time
    fast = get_next(n)                # moves two steps at a time, starts one step ahead
    while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
        slow = get_next(slow)           # advance slow by one step
        fast = get_next(get_next(fast)) # advance fast by two steps
    return fast == 1                  # true only if the fast runner reached 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = 19
    print(is_happy(n))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the sequence of numbers behaves exactly like a linked list, where each number's next value is computed by the same fixed function. If the sequence is happy, it reaches 1, and 1 always maps to itself, meaning the fast pointer, moving twice as fast, will land on 1 either at the same time as or before slow does. If the sequence is not happy, it must enter some cycle among a finite set of reachable values, and a fast pointer moving twice as fast around a cycle is mathematically guaranteed to eventually lap and land on the exact same value as the slow pointer, just like two runners on a circular track.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The sequence reaches 1","fast reaches 1, possibly before slow does, and the loop stops on that check","True, happy number"],["The sequence enters a cycle that never reaches 1","fast eventually laps slow and they land on the same non-1 value","False, not a happy number"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: get_next is factored out as its own function since it is called up to three times per outer iteration, once for slow and twice for fast, and writing that digit extraction logic three separate times would be needlessly repetitive.

fast starts one full step ahead of slow, already at get_next(n) rather than n itself, specifically so that comparing them makes sense from the very first loop check, rather than comparing a pointer to itself.

The loop condition checks fast != 1 before checking slow != fast, since reaching 1 is a valid stopping condition on its own and should not be masked by a same-value check that also happens to be true once both pointers reach 1 together.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: the same order as the brute force, bounded by how quickly the sequence reaches 1 or falls into a cycle.
Space: O(1), just two numbers being tracked, a genuine improvement over the growing set used before. This is already the theoretical floor for extra memory.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is recognizing that a sequence defined by "apply this function to get the next value" is exactly the same shape as a linked list, which means cycle detection techniques transfer directly, even though there is no actual list in sight. Floyd's tortoise and hare is a general tool worth remembering whenever a sequence like this shows up.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that the fast pointer needs to check for reaching 1 partway through its own two-step advance, not only at the very end.
Assuming any repeated number means "not happy" without confirming that repeated number is not 1 itself.
Recomputing the sum of squares incorrectly, for example squaring the whole number instead of each digit separately.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a great way to show that you recognize disguised linked list patterns. Explicitly naming it as a cycle detection problem, and connecting it to Floyd's algorithm from linked lists, demonstrates the ability to transfer a known technique to a new looking problem rather than only recognizing it in its original context.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the extra memory", think: Floyd's slow and fast pointer cycle detection, the same technique used for linked lists.
If the interviewer says "why does this relate to linked lists", think: each number points to exactly one next number, the same shape as a singly linked list.
If the interviewer says "how do you know it will always terminate", think: only finitely many values are reachable through the sum of squares function, so a repeat, and therefore a cycle, is guaranteed if 1 is never reached.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you explain why this problem is structurally the same as detecting a cycle in a linked list?
Why does the fast pointer moving twice as fast guarantee it eventually meets the slow pointer inside a cycle?
Can you describe what the one repeating cycle other than {1} looks like for this problem?
How would the approach change if you needed to find the length of the repeating cycle, not just whether one exists?
What is the maximum number of distinct values the hash set based approach could ever need to store, given the problem's input constraints?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Linked list cycle detection, Floyd's tortoise and hare, the exact same technique applied here to a sequence instead of list nodes.
Any "apply a function repeatedly" problem, where a functional sequence defined by f(x) has the same underlying graph structure as a linked list, even with no explicit nodes or pointers.
Finding the start of a cycle, or the cycle's length, both natural follow ups once basic cycle detection is understood.
Hash set based visited-tracking as the go-to first solution for any repetition or cycle detection problem, with pointer based cycle detection as the space optimized follow up.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same overall time behavior, since both walk the identical sequence of numbers. The meaningful difference is space: the hash set approach uses memory proportional to how many numbers are visited, while Floyd's cycle detection uses O(1) space regardless of how long the sequence runs.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: disguised cycle detection, a "next value" sequence with the exact same shape as a linked list.

Core Idea: treat the sum-of-squares-of-digits function as generating a linked-list-like sequence, then apply Floyd's slow and fast pointer technique to detect whether it reaches 1 or falls into a repeating cycle, with no extra memory needed.
Time: bounded by how quickly the sequence reaches 1 or a known repeating cycle, the same order for both approaches.
Space: O(k) for the hash set approach, O(1) for Floyd's cycle detection.

Most Important Observation: this problem has no list, no nodes, and no pointers on the surface, yet it is structurally identical to linked list cycle detection once each number is viewed as pointing to its own next value.
Interview Difficulty: easy to solve with a hash set, but recognizing and naming the disguised cycle detection pattern is what turns a correct answer into an impressive one.
One line memory trick: numbers pointing to numbers is still a linked list, so tortoise and hare still works.
